introduction.p: In the complex plane, multiplication can turn an arrow without changing its length. Can quaternion multiplication do the same thing for an arrow in space? There is a small obstacle: a quaternion has four real coordinates, while our arrow has only three. This project uses that extra coordinate to discover how spatial rotations work.

Work through the steps in order. Keep the quaternion multiplication table from nearby, and sketch the two-dimensional planes as they appear. You will need distributivity, the dot and cross products, and the angle-addition identities for sine and cosine. No matrix formulas are needed. Try each checkpoint before opening its hint.

Throughout the project, vectors move while the coordinate axes stay fixed. Positive spatial angles follow the right-hand rule: point your right thumb along the positive axis and curl your fingers in the direction of the turn. We use \phi for the angle in a quaternion exponential and reserve \theta for the eventual angle of rotation in three-dimensional space. Discovering their relationship is part of the work.

subsection.title: Step 1: recall how complex multiplication turns a plane
subsection.p: Use the polar expression from with the notation e^{i\phi}=\cos\phi+i\sin\phi. For the next few steps, abbreviate c=\cos\phi and s=\sin\phi. The complex plane has the ordered basis (1,i): draw 1 to the right and i upward.

li.p: Compute (c+si)1 and (c+si)i. Draw their images when \phi=\pi/6. What angle has each arrow turned?
Use distributivity to find (c+si)(x+yi). Write the resulting coordinates, and check that their squared length is x^2+y^2.
Write x+yi=r(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha). Use the angle-addition identities to show that multiplication replaces \alpha by \alpha+\phi. Why does this establish a rotation for every arrow?

hint.p: The basis images are c+si and -s+ci. In the length calculation, the mixed terms cancel and c^2+s^2=1.

subsection.p: Keep the resulting pattern in view: (x,y)\longmapsto(cx-sy,sx+cy). More generally, in a plane with ordered perpendicular unit directions (A,B), a positive turn through \phi sends A\longmapsto cA+sB,\qquad B\longmapsto-sA+cB. The order matters: a small positive angle turns the first direction toward the second. We will recognize rotations by this pattern, even when the plane sits in four dimensions.

subsection.title: Step 2: find two rotating planes inside four dimensions
subsection.p: Regard the quaternion space \mathbb H as the real coordinate space a_0+a_1i+a_2j+a_3k\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3). Its four perpendicular unit directions are 1,i,j,k. The direction 1 is a genuine coordinate direction here. It is perpendicular to the three-dimensional subspace of pure imaginary quaternions.

Each of i,j,k squares to -1. Thus each gives its own version of Euler's formula:
q_i=e^{i\phi}\amp=c+si, q_j=e^{j\phi}\amp=c+sj, q_k=e^{k\phi}\amp=c+sk.
If you recall the exponential series, this follows by grouping its even and odd powers: for E=i,j,k,
e^{E\phi}\amp=\left(1-\frac{\phi^2}{2!}+\frac{\phi^4}{4!}-\cdots\right) \amp\qquad+E\left(\phi-\frac{\phi^3}{3!}+\frac{\phi^5}{5!}-\cdots\right).
You may use the sine-cosine expressions directly for all the calculations below.

exercise.title: Multiply every basis direction on the left

statement.p: Define L_{q_i}(X)=q_iX, and similarly for q_j,q_k. Here X can be any quaternion. Verify the first row of the table and fill every question mark in the other two rows. Keep the multiplier on the left.

table.title: Images of the four basis directions under left multiplication.

li.p: For L_{q_i}, recognize the rotation pattern in the ordered planes (1,i) and (j,k). Sketch these as two separate ordinary planes. Mark the angle \phi in each.

For L_{q_j}, use the ordered planes (1,j) and (k,i). For L_{q_k}, use (1,k) and (i,j). Check that both planes in each pair turn by +\phi. Why would writing (i,k) in place of (k,i) reverse the reported sign?
Use the two perpendicular planes to explain why each map preserves |X|^2, the sum of the four squared real coordinates.

hint.p: For example, q_jk=ck+s(jk)=ck+si, while q_ji=ci+s(ji)=ci-sk. Read these as images of the ordered pair (k,i). The squared lengths of the two plane components add to the squared length in four dimensions.

exercise.title: Why is one multiplication not yet our spatial rotation?

statement.p: Compute the real part of q_i(xi+yj+zk). Then set \phi=\pi/2 and follow the input i. Does its image still represent a vector in three-dimensional space? Explain why preserving length in four dimensions does not by itself give a rotation of the pure imaginary subspace.

hint.p: The real part is -sx. In particular, ii=-1 points along the real coordinate direction.

subsection.title: Step 3: use right multiplication to control the two turns

statement.p:
For q=a_0+a_1i+a_2j+a_3k, define its quaternion conjugate and its length by
\overline q\amp=a_0-a_1i-a_2j-a_3k, |q|\amp=\sqrt{a_0^2+a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2}.
A unit quaternion has |q|=1.

li.p: Write q=a_0+V, where V=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k, and use V^2=-(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2) to prove q\overline q=\overline q q=|q|^2.
Deduce that q^{-1}=\overline q/|q|^2 for q\ne0. Check that q_i,q_j,q_k are unit quaternions. What is q_i^{-1}?

hint.p: Expand (a_0+V)(a_0-V). Real numbers commute with every quaternion, so the mixed terms cancel. For q_i, the inverse is c-si.

subsection.p: Now try the map R_{q_i^{-1}}(X)=Xq_i^{-1}=X(c-si). Because multiplication does not commute, changing sides may change the geometry.

li.p: Compute 1(c-si), i(c-si), j(c-si), and k(c-si). Compare each with the first row of .
Show that right multiplication by q_i^{-1} turns the ordered plane (1,i) through -\phi, but turns (j,k) through +\phi.
Predict what happens if you first apply L_{q_i} and then R_{q_i^{-1}}. Which plane should stop turning? Which angle should add?

hint.p: The crucial sign is ji=-k, so j(c-si)=cj-sji=cj+sk. On the other hand, i(c-si)=s+ci.

subsection.p: Record your prediction in this table before multiplying the two operations out.

subsection.title: Step 4: discover a spatial rotation and its half-angle
subsection.p: The combined operation is C_{q_i}(X)=q_iXq_i^{-1}. It is called conjugation by q_i. Distinguish this map from taking the quaternion conjugate \overline X: conjugation by a fixed quaternion means multiplying on the left by that quaternion and on the right by its inverse.

exercise.title: Check the prediction on all four directions

li.p: Compute q_i1q_i^{-1} and q_iiq_i^{-1}. Explain why both 1 and i return to their starting positions.

Complete this calculation without moving factors past one another:
q_ijq_i^{-1}\amp=(cj+sk)(c-si) \amp=c^2j-csji+sck-s^2ki.
Collect the j and k terms and use c^2-s^2=\cos(2\phi) and 2cs=\sin(2\phi).
Compute q_ikq_i^{-1} in the same way. Use distributivity to find the image of xi+yj+zk. Does any real part remain?

hint.p: Use ji=-k and ki=j in the displayed expansion. For the final part, C_{q_i}(xi+yj+zk)=xC_{q_i}(i)+yC_{q_i}(j)+zC_{q_i}(k).

subsection.p:
Check your result against the coordinate rule
(x,y,z)\longmapsto \bigl(x,\ y\cos(2\phi)-z\sin(2\phi),\ y\sin(2\phi)+z\cos(2\phi)\bigr).
The x-coordinate stays fixed, and the yz-plane follows the complex rotation pattern. Thus the pure imaginary subspace stays pure imaginary. It rotates about the +i axis, with positive motion from j toward k. The angle is 2\phi: the two four-dimensional turns cancelled in (1,i) and added in (j,k).

exercise.title: Choose the quaternion for a quarter turn

li.p: To obtain a spatial angle \theta, what value of \phi should you use? Write the quaternion for a positive \pi/2 rotation about the x-axis.
Use your quaternion to rotate V=i+2j+3k. Check your result geometrically in the yz-plane and compare the squared lengths.
If someone uses q=i=e^{i\pi/2} in qVq^{-1}, what spatial angle do they actually get? Test the input j.
Why would the analogous complex expression e^{i\phi}ze^{-i\phi} leave every complex number z unchanged?

hint.p: A spatial quarter turn needs q=(1+i)/\sqrt2 and gives i-3j+2k in the second part. Complex numbers commute, so their two multipliers can be brought together and cancelled.

subsection.title: Step 5: rotate about the other coordinate axes
subsection.p: Return to your rows for q_j and q_k in . The same cancellation-and-addition mechanism should work, with the quaternion units in cyclic order.

exercise.title: Use cyclic order to keep the signs straight

li.p: For q_j=c+sj, compute the four images under right multiplication by c-sj. Compare the turns in (1,j) and (k,i) with left multiplication. Then find all four images under X\longmapsto q_jXq_j^{-1}.
Repeat for q_k=c+sk, using (1,k) and (i,j).
Replace 2\phi by \theta. Write coordinate rules for rotating (x,y,z) about the y- and z-axes.
Check positive quarter turns: about +j, k should move to i; about +k, i should move to j. Where do the other two coordinate directions go in each case?

hint.p: For the y-axis, the coordinate rule is (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\cos\theta+z\sin\theta,\ y,\ -x\sin\theta+z\cos\theta). For the z-axis, it is (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta,\ x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta,\ z). In each case the coordinate along the axis stays fixed.

subsection.title: Step 6: build the same two planes around any axis
subsection.p: A rotation axis need not be a coordinate axis. Choose a unit vector \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2,u_3) and represent it by U=u_1i+u_2j+u_3k,\qquad u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2=1. The identity in gives U^2=-1. Thus U can play the role of an imaginary unit, and q=e^{U\phi}=\cos\phi+U\sin\phi=c+sU is a unit quaternion with inverse c-sU.

exercise.title: Make a basis suited to the chosen axis

statement.p: Choose any unit vector \mathbf b perpendicular to \mathbf u, write its pure imaginary quaternion as B, and set W=UB.

li.p: Use the scalar-vector product identity UB=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf u\times\mathbf b to explain why W is pure imaginary and corresponds to the unit vector \mathbf u\times\mathbf b. Why are 1,U,B,W four mutually perpendicular unit directions?
Use the same product identity to prove BU=-UB=-W. Then use associativity to show UW=-B,\qquad WU=B. You have recovered the multiplication relations needed for two rotating planes.
Compute the images of 1,U,B,W under left multiplication by c+sU and under right multiplication by c-sU. Identify the angles in the ordered planes (1,U) and (B,W).

Combine the two maps. Show that conjugation fixes 1,U and sends
B\amp\longmapsto\cos(2\phi)B+\sin(2\phi)W, W\amp\longmapsto-\sin(2\phi)B+\cos(2\phi)W.
Why is positive motion from B toward W=UB the right-hand direction about \mathbf u?

hint.p: First, UW=U(UB)=U^2B=-B and WU=(UB)U=U(BU)=-U(UB)=B. Then qB=cB+sW, while Bq^{-1}=cB-sBU=cB+sW. Both operations turn the (B,W) plane in the same direction.

subsection.p: We have reduced the general axis to the same picture as the i-axis. Every spatial vector is a real linear combination of U,B,W. Conjugation fixes its component along U and rotates its perpendicular component in (B,W). The real coordinate stays zero. Since the three spatial basis directions are perpendicular unit vectors, this operation preserves lengths and angles and gives a rotation about the line through the origin in direction \mathbf u.

subsection.title: Step 7: turn the discovery into a usable formula
subsection.p:
You can now assemble the rotation rule. For a desired angle \theta about a unit axis \mathbf u, use the half-angle:
q\amp=\cos\frac{\theta}{2}+U\sin\frac{\theta}{2}, q^{-1}=\overline q\amp=\cos\frac{\theta}{2}-U\sin\frac{\theta}{2}.
Encode \mathbf v=(x,y,z) as V=xi+yj+zk, and compute \boxed{V'=qV\overline q.} The coefficients of i,j,k in V' are the rotated vector's coordinates.

exercise.title: Recover a formula using dot and cross products

li.p:
Split the vector into components parallel and perpendicular to the axis:
\mathbf v_{\parallel}=(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)\mathbf u,\qquad \mathbf v_{\perp}=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_{\parallel}.
Check that \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v_{\perp}=0.

When \mathbf v_{\perp}\ne\mathbf0, choose \mathbf b=\mathbf v_{\perp}/\|\mathbf v_{\perp}\| in Step 6. Use the image of B to obtain
\mathbf v'=\mathbf v_{\parallel}+\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_{\perp} +\sin\theta\,(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v_{\perp}).
Explain separately why this also holds when \mathbf v_{\perp}=\mathbf0.

Substitute the component formulas and use \mathbf u\times\mathbf v_{\parallel}=\mathbf0 to derive
\mathbf v'\amp=\cos\theta\,\mathbf v +(1-\cos\theta)(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)\mathbf u \amp\qquad+\sin\theta\,(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v).
This is called Rodrigues' rotation formula. Explain geometrically why the axis component and the length are preserved.

hint.p: The two perpendicular vectors \mathbf v_{\perp} and \mathbf u\times\mathbf v_{\perp} have equal length. Their sine-cosine combination is precisely the plane rotation already discovered.

example.title: A half turn about a tilted axis

statement.p:
Rotate \mathbf v=(1,0,0) through \theta=\pi about \mathbf u=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2. Here U=\frac{i+j}{\sqrt2},\qquad q=U,\qquad\overline q=-U. Direct multiplication gives
qiq^{-1}\amp=\frac{(-1-k)(-i-j)}{2} \amp=\frac{i+j+ki+kj}{2}=j.
Thus (1,0,0) becomes (0,1,0). The vector formula agrees: \mathbf v'=-\mathbf v+2(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)\mathbf u =-(1,0,0)+(1,1,0)=(0,1,0). The half turn keeps the component along the tilted axis and reverses the perpendicular component.

subsection.title: Step 8: test the construction and tell its geometric story

exercise.title: Three checks on your rotation rule

li.p: Rotate through 2\pi/3 about \mathbf u=(1,1,1)/\sqrt3. Show that q=(1+i+j+k)/2, and compute the images of i,j,k by conjugation. Use them to rotate i+2j+3k. Check the length and the component along the axis.
Show that q and -q give exactly the same map V\longmapsto qVq^{-1}. What quaternion does the half-angle rule produce for \theta=2\pi, and why is the resulting spatial map the identity?

Let q_x=(1+i)/\sqrt2 and q_y=(1+j)/\sqrt2. Starting with k, apply the x-axis quarter turn and then the y-axis quarter turn. Reverse the order and compare. Use associativity to show that the first order is represented by q_yq_x: q_y(q_xVq_x^{-1})q_y^{-1}=(q_yq_x)V(q_x^{-1}q_y^{-1}). Verify that the last two factors form (q_yq_x)^{-1}.

hint.p: The first rotation cycles i\mapsto j\mapsto k\mapsto i. For the third part, the two orders send k to -j and i, respectively. A quaternion product encodes the first rotation in its rightmost factor.

subsection.p: Your project report. Present the construction so that another student could use it without memorizing an unexplained formula. Include:

li.p: Your complex-plane sketch and completed basis-image table for left multiplication by e^{i\phi},e^{j\phi},e^{k\phi}.
Two plane sketches for the i-axis case, with arrows showing the left and right turns. Explain where the angles cancel and where they add.
A derivation of the half-angle rule and an explanation of why qVq^{-1} stays pure imaginary and fixes the chosen axis.
One coordinate-axis rotation and one tilted-axis rotation, computed with quaternions and checked using dot and cross products.

A short set of instructions: normalize a nonzero axis vector, form the unit quaternion with half the desired angle, encode the input vector, multiply in the order qV\overline q, and read off the three coefficients.

subsection.p: Optional extension. Rotate a point P about a line through a point A with unit direction \mathbf u. Explain why you should apply the quaternion rule to the displacement P-A and then add A back.

conclusion.p: Complex multiplication supplied the plane-rotation pattern. Quaternion multiplication placed that pattern in two perpendicular planes at once. Multiplication by the inverse on the right cancelled the turn involving the real coordinate and doubled the turn perpendicular to the chosen axis. That is the geometric reason a unit quaternion with angle \theta/2 produces a spatial rotation through \theta.
